generatedProse.concept-context: A psychology exam often asks you to evaluate theories or analyse a scenario under time pressure, so exam-day strategy decides how much of your revision reaches the page. Arriving settled and reading the whole paper first stop you writing everything you know about a keyword instead of answering the question asked. Dividing time by the marks, and planning a brief argument before writing, protect the critical, evaluative answers psychology rewards.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students, equally well revised, sit the same two-hour exam with two essay questions.

Tom arrives just in time and hurries to his desk, flustered. With one pen and no watch, he scans the paper, recognises the word memory in the first question, and writes everything he knows about memory models. That answer runs well over an hour, so the second question, on attachment, is rushed and half planned. His knowledge was there; his strategy let it leak away.

Amara arrives early, lays out her pens and a watch, and reads both questions before choosing. Seeing they carry equal marks, she gives each an hour, spends ten minutes planning an argument, and writes to that plan. When time runs short on the second essay, she closes it with a brief conclusion rather than leaving it unfinished. Her preparation showed because her time was controlled.

Both knew the material. Only Amara protected that knowledge with timing and a calm start, and so turned it into a complete paper.
generatedProse.summary: Exam-day strategy is how prepared psychology knowledge becomes marks. You can now explain how an organised approach manages anxiety and protects performance, analyse contrasting approaches to spot the decisions that matter, and devise a timed plan for an exam of your own. With active revision behind you and a clear plan for the day, your preparation has the best chance to show.

check.body: In the worked example, which decision most clearly cost Tom marks?

items.text: Spending well over an hour on the first essay, which left the second rushed.
Arriving a few minutes before the start.
Recognising the word memory in the first question.
Bringing only one pen to the exam.

feedback.correct: That's right. Letting the first essay run well over an hour left too little time for the second.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the decision about how Tom spent his time across the two essays.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The clearest cost was spending well over an hour on the first essay, which left the second rushed. The late arrival and single pen added stress but did not directly lose the marks.
